The primary focus of sports cardiology is the health and safety of athletes. Sudden
cardiac death is potentially preventable, which makes identification and management of
a manageable cause of utmost importance. This chapter reviews the most common
causes of sudden cardiac death in this patient population and the role of
preparticipation physical evaluation and screening.
Preparticipation Physical Evaluation and Screening

Preparticipation Physical Evaluation and Screening
Exercise is associated with substantial short- and long-term health benefits, and athletes
generally are viewed as one of the healthiest patient populations. Regardless, an
exercise paradox exists: vigorous athletic activity may transiently increase the risk of an
athlete succumbing to sudden cardiac death if he or she has an underlying
cardiovascular disorder. Unfortunately, sudden cardiac death may be the first and only
sign or manifestation of an underlying cardiovascular disorder in an otherwise
asymptomatic individual. An athlete’s tragic and unexpected death during a sporting
event or practice generates considerable attention and publicity, prompting questions
about the importance of preparticipation physical evaluation and screening.
Organizations such as the American Heart Association, the American College of
Cardiology, and the American Medical Society for Sports Medicine view preparticipation
physical evaluation and screening as a necessary tool to detect silent cardiovascular
abnormalities that may lead to sudden cardiac death.1,2,3 Detecting these abnormalities
creates the opportunity to manage them and to modify risk factors to protect the health
and well-being of this patient population.
All organizations agree that a thorough patient history and physical evaluation are
necessary. Some organizations recommend screening electrocardiography (ECG);
however, this is not standard practice. In addition, the literature remains divided on the
sensitivity and specificity of ECG as a tool to screen for potential causes of sudden
cardiac death.4

Obtaining an accurate medical and family history and performing a cardiac-focused
physical examination are simple first steps in screening athletes for potential causes of
sudden cardiac arrest. Based on the scientific statement from the American College of
Cardiology and the American Heart Association, the following 14 points should be
included in the screening of athletes for potential causes of sudden cardiac
arrest5 (Table 1).
Table 1 The 14-Element American Heart Association Recommendations for
Preparticipation
Medical history
Personal history
1. Chest pain/discomfort/tightness/pressure related to exertion
2. Unexplained syncope/near-syncope
3. Excessive and unexplained dyspnea/fatigue or palpitations associated with exercise
4. Prior recognition of a heart murmur
5. Elevated systemic blood pressure
6. Prior restriction from participation in sports
7. Prior testing for the heart ordered by a physician
Family history
8. Premature death (sudden and unexpected or otherwise) before age 50 yr
attributable to heart disease in one or more relative
9. Disability from heart disease in close relative younger than 50 yr
10. Hypertrophic or dilated cardiomyopathy, long QT syndrome, or other ion
channelopathy, Marfan syndrome, or clinically important arrhythmias; specific
knowledge of genetic cardiac conditions in family members.
Physical examination
11. Heart murmur

Red Flags
Although not universally recommended, a screening ECG should be interpreted by an
experienced sports cardiologist/electrophysiologist. Such interpretation helps prevent
unnecessary sports restriction and additional investigation by helping to distinguish
physiologic cardiac adaptation from findings of underlying cardiac disease.
Sudden Cardiac Death

Sudden Cardiac Death
The estimated incidence of sudden cardiac death in young athletes has been reported to
be approximately 2.3 in 100,000 athletes per year, with most deaths in athletes younger
than 35 years being secondary to an inherited or congenital, structural, or electrical
disorder of the heart.6 In young athletes, the following are among the most common
causes of sudden cardiac death:
HCM
Coronary artery anomalies
Long QT syndrome
Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy
Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT)
Myocarditis

Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
Epidemiology and clinical presentation
Characterized by a thickened but not dilated left ventricle in the absence of another cardiac
or systemic disease (ie, aortic valve stenosis, systemic hypertension) (Figure 1).
HCM is the most common genetic heart disease with an autosomal dominant inheritance
pattern.7
HCM accounts for approximately 27% of sudden death in young athletes.8
One-third of patients with HCM have no or mild obstruction of the left ventricular outflow
tract at rest or with exercise.
During adolescence, as body growth accelerates, genetically affected individuals often show
striking spontaneous increase in ventricular wall thickness, which is characteristically
asymmetrical, usually with increased septal thickening.
Heart failure may become evident at any age. The predominant complaint is exercise
intolerance because of dyspnea and/or fatigue. Chest pain also is noted and may be a
manifestation of myocardial ischemia.
Episodes of impaired consciousness (syncope or near syncope) may increase suspicion for
risk of sudden cardiac death. Sudden cardiac death is believed to be the result of fatal
arrhythmias.

Diagnosis
Diagnosed via echocardiography
Echocardiography is used to differentiate the hypertrophic cardiomyopathic heart from an
athletic heart
ECG is abnormal in 90% to 95% of patients with this disease; however, no characteristic ECG
pattern is predictive of future events.
Sarcomere genetic variants are observed in 40% to 60% of patients with HCM. Therefore, the
utility of genetic testing to determine etiology and inheritance pattern has increased.
Risk stratification and sudden cardiac death
Currently, the greatest risk for sudden death in patients with HCM appears to be associated
with the following clinical red flags:
Prior cardiac arrest or sustained ventricular tachycardia
Family history of sudden cardiac death

Unexplained syncope
Massive degree of left ventricular hypertrophy (maximum wall thickness >30 mm via
echocardiography)
Hypotension or attenuated blood pressure response to exercise
Management
Pharmacotherapy aimed at slowing the heart rate and/or decreasing contractility may
improve symptoms
In select patients with evidence of increased risk of sudden death, prevention of sudden
death via an implanted cardioverter/defibrillator (ICD) is the only therapeutic option known
to alter clinical course and extend life.
Activity restrictions
Current recommendations are that athletes with HCM should be excluded from most
competitive sports except those that require low static and dynamic exertion.
Prophylactic ICDs should not be placed in athlete-patients with HCM for the sole or primary
purpose of permitting participation in high-intensity sports competition because of the
possibility of device-related complications.9
Coronary Artery Anomalies
Epidemiology and clinical presentation
Coronary artery anomalies are thought to cause 14% of sudden cardiac arrests in athletes.8
The most common coronary anomaly is the abnormal origin of the left coronary artery
arising from the right coronary artery or the abnormal origin of the right coronary artery
originating from the left coronary artery.
Occasionally, an athlete may present with chest pain, palpitations, or syncope related to
exercise; however, most patients will be asymptomatic and have a normal physical
examination.
Risk of sudden death appears to be higher with anomalous origins of the left coronary artery
than of the right coronary artery.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis is made via echocardiography and advanced cardiac imaging studies.
Treatment and activity restrictions
Management depends on the underlying coronary artery anomaly.
Management can range from continued observation without physical restriction to
restriction from all competitive sports to surgical correction with close cardiac follow-up.

Long QT Syndrome
Epidemiology and clinical presentation
Long QT syndrome is a congenital or acquired repolarization abnormality that may lead to
sudden cardiac death via the development of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (torsades
de pointes).
Known genetic mutations account for as many as 75% of cases of long QT syndrome.7 The
QT interval also may be acquired or occur secondary to medications, drugs, or metabolic
disturbances.
According to US data, mortality from long QT syndrome in athletes is approximately 2%.10
The three most common genetic variants that cause congenital long QT syndrome are
LQT1: Mutation in the potassium channel (KCNQ1) of cardiac myocyte; often triggered by
physical exertion (ie, swimming, sprinting). Risk factors include a corrected QT interval
greater than 500 ms via ECG and prior syncope. Adolescent males and post-gestation
females have a higher risk.
LQT2: Mutation in the potassium channel (KCNH2); often triggered by sudden startle from
rest or sleep. Risk factors are the same as those for LQT1. Females older than 13 years have
a higher risk.
LQT3: Mutation in the sodium channel (SCN5A) of cardiac myocytes; arrhythmias typically
occur during time of rest.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis is made via ECG, manifested as a prolonged corrected QT interval, and can be
confirmed via genetic testing.
Management
Mainstays of therapy are ß-blocker medications, avoidance of activities that trigger events,
and QT-prolonging medications. ICD implantation is recommended for those who are
survivors of cardiac arrest or who have recurrent syncope with ß-blocker therapy.
Left cardiac sympathetic denervation may be considered if ß-blocker therapy is ineffective or
not tolerated.
Activity restrictions
Participation in competitive sports is determined by phenotype and genotype after
institution of appropriate management and precautionary measures.
Competitive swimming is discouraged in symptomatic patients with LQT1.

WPW Syndrome
Epidemiology and clinical presentation
WPW syndrome is a cardiac conduction disorder characterized by abnormal accessory
conduction pathways between the atria and the ventricles.
WPW syndrome accounts for at least 1% of sudden cardiac death in athletes and may be the
first manifestation of the underlying conduction disease.8
Symptomatic patients who do not present with sudden cardiac death may present with
palpitations, pre-syncope, or syncope that results from supraventricular tachycardia (atrial
arrhythmia).
Accessory pathways with rapid repolarization (resetting) properties are more likely to be
associated with rapid conduction of atrial fibrillation, which may degenerate to ventricular
fibrillation (fatal arrhythmia).
Prediction of risk for sudden cardiac death is difficult; however, high-risk factors include male
sex, age younger than 30 years, history of atrial fibrillation, prior syncope, family history of
WPW syndrome, and associated congenital heart disease.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis is based on ECG changes: ventricular preexcitation (short PR interval, delta wave)
and rapid palpitations. Occasionally, the presumptive diagnosis is made via an incidental
finding of ventricular preexcitation on ECG.
Athletes who present with preexcitation and history of syncope or near syncope should be
restricted from physical activity until they have been evaluated by a
cardiologist/electrophysiologist.
Exercise testing has been used for risk stratification. The test helps evaluate for loss of
ventricular preexcitation suggestive of lower risk for life-threatening arrhythmias.
Risk stratification with invasive electrophysiologic studies has been proposed for
asymptomatic younger athletes engaged in moderate- to high-intensity competitive sports.
Management
Symptomatic athletes also should be considered for catheter ablation therapy of the
accessory pathway before returning to sport.
Electrophysiology studies with catheter ablation may be curative.
Activity restrictions
Dependent on the elected treatment option and risk stratification.

Epidemiology and clinical presentation
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is caused by a mutation in cardiac
desmosomes, which attach heart muscle cells to one another. Without normal desmosomes,
the heart muscles cells detach from one another and die, particularly if the heart is under
stress, such as during vigorous exercise. The damaged heart muscle cells are replaced by fat
and scar tissue, which may lead to decreased ventricular contractility, ventricular
enlargement, and increased risk of ventricular arrhythmias.
Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy accounts for approximately 2% of sudden
cardiac death in young athletes.8
Although the right and left ventricle may be at risk for this desmosomal disease, the right
ventricle is most often affected.
Most cases are familial, with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis is made via echocardiography, ECG, and advanced cardiac imaging studies.
Diagnostic criteria have been established.11
Management
Management is driven by arrhythmia burden and heart failure severity and may include anti-
arrhythmic medications, ICD placement, and heart transplantation.
Activity restrictions
Participation in most competitive sports is not recommended, with the possible exception of
low-intensity class 1A sports. Prophylactic ICD placement to permit sports participation is not
recommended.
Catecholaminergic Polymorphic Ventricular Tachycardia
Epidemiology and clinical presentation
CPVT is a condition characterized by an abnormal heart rhythm during increased adrenergic
states (excitement, exertion) caused by abnormal trafficking of calcium from the
sarcoplasmic reticulum.
As the heart rate’s increases in relation to adrenergic stimulation or exercise, it may trigger
premature ventricular complexes and runs of numerous morphologies with possible
progression to polymorphic ventricular tachycardia.
Autosomal dominant inheritance accounts for 50% to 60% of CPVT, the most common of
which is linked to the ryanodine receptor (RYR2).
Diagnosis

Exercise treadmill testing can detect as many 80% of patients with CPVT, manifested as
polymorphic ventricular ectopy during increased heart rates.
Management
Beta-blocker therapy is highly effective in decreasing life-threatening arrhythmias in patients
with CPVT. Flecainide also is effective as an adjunct to ß-blockers.
Sympathetic denervation and/or ICDs have been used in patients who have experienced
cardiac arrest, recurrent syncope, or recurrent ventricular tachycardia despite optimal
medical therapy.
Of note, electrical cardioversion (such as that from an ICD or automated external
defibrillator) may increase adrenaline release, which may result in further ventricular
tachycardia.
Activity restrictions
Avoidance of competitive sports and strenuous activity is recommended in athletes with
exercise-induced premature ventricular contractions or non-sustained ventricular
tachycardia.
Myocarditis
Epidemiology and clinical presentation
Myocarditis is defined as an inflammatory disease of the heart muscle, and it may occur
secondary to infection, inflammation, or toxins.
It has been linked to 5% to 25% of sudden cardiac death in athletes.8
The clinical presentation of patients with myocarditis is highly variable. The patient usually is
described as previously healthy, with the exception of a recent viral illness in the weeks
leading up to presentation.
The patient may present with acute heart failure, sinus tachycardia without symptoms,
arrhythmias (atrial or ventricular), heart block, acute myocardial infarction, or sudden cardiac
death.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis can be made via ECG (abnormal depolarization and/or repolarization),
echocardiography, laboratory evaluation, cardiac MRI, and cardiac biopsy (occasionally).
Management
Management is supportive and, in severe cases, may include extracorporeal membrane
oxygenation.
Activity restrictions

Athletes diagnosed with myocarditis should be restricted from exercise for 3 to 6 months to
promote resolution of inflammation, depending on clinical severity and duration of illness.
Commotio Cordis
Epidemiology and clinical presentation
Commotio cordis is an abrupt arrhythmogenic cause of sudden death and occurs as a result
of blunt-force trauma to the chest during the vulnerable ventricular repolarization period.
Commotio cordis is rare because it requires the blunt trauma to occur at a critical period
during repolarization (near the peak of the T-wave), wherein it can precipitate potentially
fatal ventricular fibrillation.
It is most commonly observed in adolescent baseball players but is possible with any physical
activity that may result in blunt-force trauma to the anterior chest wall.
Commotio cordis accounts for as much as 20% of sudden cardiac death in athletes.8
Chest protectors and softer core baseballs decrease but do not eliminate the risk of sudden
cardiac death.
Survival rates often are low unless prompt cardiopulmonary resuscitation and, more
importantly, early defibrillation is initiated.
Activity restrictions
Athletes who survive may return to sport if no residual underlying cardiac abnormality is
identified. An ECG is recommended to rule out the possibility of long QT syndrome.
